comments.text:
Hepatitis B vaccine is given 24 hours of birth (often in the first few hours, before hospital discharge) because 
	•	Protects the newborn from unrecognized maternal infection (hepatitis B surface antigen does not appear immediately after mother is infected)
	•	Prevents household or caregiver transmission (nail clippers, minor cuts n abrasions.. baby skin is fragile)
	•	Dramatically reduces the risk of chronic hepatitis B, which is highest when infection occurs in infancy
	•	If the mother is hepatitis B–positive or status unknown:
	•	The baby receives both:
	•	Hepatitis B vaccine (within 12–24 hours)
	•	as well as HBIG (hepatitis B immune globulin) within 12 hours
	•	If the mother is confirmed negative:
	•	The baby still receives the birth dose (vaccine only), because, as noted, maternal testing cannot eliminate all risk and risk if infected with hepatitis B for a newborn is very high for leading to high risk for liver failure/cirrhosis and liver cancer.

I try to look at the brighter side of things. What gives me some comfort is that people are finally asking questions again, and I genuinely hope critical thinking makes a comeback in this country. I didn’t even know my newborns were given the Hep B vaccine—I wasn’t asked or informed, and while I could have researched it myself, you expect to be able to trust doctors to communicate clearly and act in your best interest.

After being diagnosed with Hashimoto’s at 21, needing hip replacements at 37, and spending years in pain without anyone really listening or asking the right questions, it’s hard not to feel dismissed by the medical system. You live in your own body—you know when something is wrong.

I’m not anti-vaccine, and I don’t think vaccines should be eliminated. But I do think asking questions and encouraging informed consent matters. Even if we don’t all agree, at least these conversations are happening—and that’s a good thing.

transcript: If you just heard that RFK Jr. cut the childhood vaccine schedule and your brain went, "Wait, did we just lose access to vaccines?" Take a breath. Let's break down what actually changed and why it matters. On January 5th, the CDC announced a headline change. They are no longer universally recommending several vaccines for all children the way it previously did. Instead, this new schedule sorts vaccines into three buckets. One, vaccines recommended for all kids. two vaccines for certain high-risisk groups and three vaccines that fall into a category that are now shared clinical decisionmaking. Well, what moved out of the everyone gets it bucket? Influenza, roto virus, RSV, hepatitis A, hepatitis B, and menitis vaccines. Folks, these are not benign conditions. Flu hospitalizations are the highest they've been in a decade. 50 to 70,000 kids were hospitalized with roto virus before the vaccine was around. Hepatitis B is especially serious for babies as they have a 90% chance of developing chronic infection which can lead to cerosis or even cancer later in life. Actually about 20,000 kids got hepatitis B every year before the universal vaccine and half of those were not from the mother. So no testing doesn't solve the problem completely. Recommending certain vaccines targeted at high-risisk groups sometimes can absolutely make sense, but only if the data points in that direction. And I need to state this clearly. No breakthrough or new research was discovered to make this change. And vaccines remain proven to be safe to be given to healthy children at scale to prevent illness. So, how did the committees put in charge of our children's well-being allow this change? Well, they didn't. No independent body reviewed and recommended these changes. It was a unilateral and truly not scientific decision criticized by CDC's own employees and medical experts across the country. And here's why this is a big deal. Universal recommendations aren't just words on a website. They drive what our medical offices stock, what parents view as standard, what schools and states consider, and what communities actually do. In public health, even small drops in vaccine uptake can mean [music] big increases in outbreaks. I'm not one to fearmonger, but here's the harsh reality. Less children will be vaccinated. More children will get sick. You will hear news of more unnecessary hospitalizations [music] and deaths in the unvaccinated. So, what should you do as a parent or caregiver? Don't panic. Look to professional organizations like the AFP and AAP. Call your doctor. Ask, "What do you recommend given my child's age, risks, and local disease spread?" And if you're hearing loud voices online, [music] remember protecting the well-being of children shouldn't be political. It's clinical.
